She'll definitely get to the run-off election. The first round in France will be ELECTRIC! It usually is, and crazy things happen all of the time, but this year it's already happening and there are as many as six legitimate candidates with a shot to get into the two-person final vote. France also controls elections and campaigning significantly and it shortens the campaign greatly. The month prior to the first round vote is when things get interesting.

As it stands, Le Pen's chances depend greatly of course on who gets in against her in the final round. The assumption by the establishment and their parrots is that the country will united against her as they did against her father in 2002. That's a very stupid assumption as she's not her father, he was running against the sitting President who was not a total lame duck, and the times have changed, too. Marine Le Pen's party is very different from the one her father controlled and the times are also very different. Her father never had her levels of support and he only got into the second round on a fluke because the Socialists (largest left party) ran a weak candidate and the left vote was split amongst all of the other candidates.

French politics are different from the US. Most importantly, there are multiple parties with real voting blocks of 5-10% and sometimes as high as 20-30% with a particular candidate. Also, with the two-party system and the generally higher level of attention paid by the public and investment/knowledge of politics, it's possible for surprises to occur. A major factor is that the French seem to prefer candidates they know well and who have been around a while - this is a strike against the newer faces you'll hear about and helps the people who've been involved in national politics for decades. This is because the French assume all politicians are corrupt and vile liars and after they've been around awhile it's easier to know what manner their corruption takes and people decide if they can live with that. New people can end up doing really shady things and so it's very difficult for them to get into the top office. Le Pen is a known figure, for context, and this helps her.

The campaign has already been rocked by the "primaries" for the two major parties. Fillon is the "republican" candidate, much to the surprise of most people. This was a huge blunder on their part as they assume he can just adopt as many of Le Pen's positions as needed to trick voters into voting for him (Sarkozy employed this strategy against her father in 2007). The problem is that Fillon's economic plans are EXTREMELY unpopular in France, as in "never gonna happen" unpopular. In a context of Fillon/Le Pen I think she has a pretty good shot of beating him even though the media/press/parrots will tell you he's the best person to beat her.

Anyone else who gets in will be running entirely against her nationalism/foreign policy. Basically "le racist meme" will be the substance of the election. It will be interesting to see who wins the Socialist run-off in a couple of days. That primary featured a surprise, Hamon, against Valls, a former prime minster and probably the most "establishment/globalist" candidate in the race. Valls is the guy the powers that be want in there against Le Pen, but the French are clearly on to him and Hamon is looking to have a good shot at winning the socialist primary. He's a former education minster and will play the "good socalist/Trudeau" role but without the star power. YOU WANT HIM TO WIN THE SOCALIST PRIMARY. Valls is much more credible for President in France.

What happens next is the general election, where EVERYONE gets a shot. In France, these candidates get public funding, TV time, and ads. Their message does get out there. With Hamon, Fillon, and Le Pen, the other two key candidates are Emmanuel Macron (former socialist government member with his own independent party) and Jean-Luc Melanchon. Plus a couple more leftists with a shot at votes.

What you have in France is an utterly failed Socialist party president Hollande who isn't even running for re-election because he would be sure to lose. He's hated by the left probably more than the right in that he basically did badly for two years then lost the "midterm" elections and immediately sold out (this is where Valls came into power as Prime Minster). The left will probably see massive fracturing in the vote this year as French voters are strategic and smart. They are fairly sure the Socialist candidate won't win (only Valls voters, the Clinton archetype, believe otherwise). What happens then is people are free to vote for their true preferred/niche candidates. I expect to see the left vote for all kinds of people and end up with like four people getting 10%. Fillon has a built-in block of voters more or less, and should be able to do ok in the first round with 20-30%. Le Pen seems to have around 35% support in the polling going into the first round, almost assuring her to get into the run-off.

The key will be how Fillon does. If he fails to excite voters who are feeling "free" to vote their hearts in the first round,his numbers could be very disappointing. Sub-20% would be a near death blow. The thing is that he could be weak, but still have the largest unified block because of Socialist fracturing. This is the best case scenario, as in the second round he will have a hard time getting the scattered left parties to support his radical policy proposals. Le Pen, on the other hand, has a much easier time appealing to the left on economic grounds.

Now, the REAL best case scenario is the Socialists pick Hamon, the momentum candidate, this week. He gets hyped up as the "rising star" and they all jerk themselves off thinking he can do this ala Sanders. Combined with weak Fillon support, he could muster say 20% and SNEAK INTO THE SECOND ROUND. This is EXACTLY how Le Pen's father got into the 2nd round in 2002, fyi, so it's very possible.

Here's the kicker - he's young, relatively inexperienced, and represents the disaffected left-wing of the Socialist party. But he's still in their very tainted party and the OTHER half of the socialists really aren't fond of him (the Valls block) and basically are becoming more centrist. This means his ceiling is possibly very low even if enthusiasm is high. Le Pen compared to Hamon appears to be a mature statesman, long-known to the public, proposing few radical changes other than anti-eu/nationalism. I think she beats him easily.

Macron is the strongest candidate against Le Pen in my mind without question. The hope is that his voters get sucked into Hamon hype and he fails to get into the second round. Macron is the establishment's "fail-safe" against Valls not getting in. He will try to usurp all of the populist hype but is pro-EU/establishment in that respect. He's credible to the left because he told the Socialists to fuck off when Hollande sold out. He's a good face for TV and is the real "Trudeau" candidate. French aren't as dumb as Canadians, fortunately, and Macron/Le Pen will be a pure referendum on the EU.
